We begin with the definition of distributional equivalence (Quote 4 & 5), asserting that identically distributed integrable functions yield identical expectations. This forms the baseline for treating independent trials symmetrically. Next, we introduce the core mechanism of averaging: the L2 convergence of sums of independent functions (Quote 1, 2, 3). Because variance is additive for independent variables and homogeneous of degree 2, the variance of the sample mean scales inversely with the square of the sample size. If the individual variances are bounded, the variance of the average vanishes as n approaches infinity. This L2 convergence strictly implies convergence in measure, guaranteeing that extreme deviations become exponentially rare. Finally, the elementary analysis lemma (Quote 9, 10) provides the deterministic counterpart: if a sequence converges pointwise, its Cesaro mean converges to the same limit. In our sovereign primitive framework, this duality allows us to treat stochastic sports data as a hybrid system. We use the distributional invariance to normalize disparate athlete metrics, apply the L2 variance decay to quantify the reliability of aggregate team statistics, and utilize the Cesaro lemma to smooth noisy, high-frequency telemetry into actionable, low-frequency strategic signals. The failure modes arise precisely when independence is violated (e.g., clustered injuries) or when variances are infinite (e.g., outlier-heavy scoring systems like certain fantasy leagues).
